title: Dr. Heidegger’s Experiment
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne (retold)
summary: 風変わりな老医師が、四人の老人の友人に「若返りの泉」の水を飲ませる実験をします。若さを取り戻した彼らは、何を学ぶのか。ホーソーンの寓意的短編。

source.note: Retold with simplified vocabulary from Nathaniel Hawthorne’s “Dr. Heidegger’s Experiment” (1837, public domain).

paragraphs: That very strange man, old Dr. Heidegger, once invited four elderly friends to meet him in his study. There were three white-bearded gentlemen, Mr. Medbourne, Colonel Killigrew and Mr. Gascoigne, and a thin old lady whose husband had died long ago, and who was called the Widow Wycherly. They were all melancholy old creatures who had been unfortunate in life, and whose greatest misfortune was that they were not long ago in their graves.

Mr. Medbourne, in the strength of his youth, had been a successful merchant, but he had lost everything through a foolish business gamble, and was now little better than a beggar. Colonel Killigrew had wasted his best years, his health and his money in the pursuit of pleasure, which had left him with gout and other kinds of pain in body and soul. Mr. Gascoigne was a ruined politician, a man with a bad reputation, or at least he had had one, until time had buried him from the knowledge of the present generation and made him obscure instead of infamous. As for the Widow Wycherly, tradition tells us that she had been a great beauty in her day. But for a long time now she had lived alone, because certain scandalous stories had turned the people of the town against her.

It is worth mentioning that each of these three old gentlemen, Mr. Medbourne, Colonel Killigrew and Mr. Gascoigne, had once been in love with the Widow Wycherly, and they had once been on the point of cutting each other’s throats for her sake.

Dr. Heidegger’s study was a dim, old-fashioned room, full of cobwebs and dust. Around the walls stood oak bookcases, filled with huge old books. In the center of the room hung a black mirror in a gold frame, and people said that the spirits of all the doctor’s dead patients lived inside it and stared at him whenever he looked into it. On another wall hung a full-length portrait of a young lady, dressed in silk, with a face as faded as her dress. More than half a century before, Dr. Heidegger had been about to marry this young lady. But she had become slightly ill and swallowed one of her lover’s prescriptions, and she had died on the evening before their wedding.

On the summer afternoon of our story, a small round table stood in the middle of the room. On it was a beautiful cut-glass vase. The sunshine came through the window and fell on the vase, so that a soft glow was reflected from it onto the gray faces of the five old people sitting around it. Four champagne glasses were also on the table.
“My dear old friends,” said Dr. Heidegger, “may I ask your help in one of those little experiments with which I amuse myself here in my study?”

Without waiting for a reply, he hobbled across the room and returned with a large, black book. From its pages he took a dried rose, so brown and crumbly that it seemed it would turn to dust in his fingers.

“This rose,” said Dr. Heidegger, with a sigh, “this same withered and crumbling flower, bloomed fifty-five years ago. It was given to me by Sylvia Ward, whose portrait hangs over there, and I meant to wear it on our wedding day. For fifty-five years it has been kept between the pages of this old book. Now, do you think it possible that this rose of half a century could ever bloom again?”
“Nonsense!” said the Widow Wycherly, with an impatient shake of her head. “You might as well ask whether an old woman’s wrinkled face could ever bloom again.”
“See!” answered Dr. Heidegger.

He removed the cover of the vase and threw the faded rose into the water it contained. At first it lay lightly on the surface of the water. Soon, however, a strange change began to be visible. The crushed and dried petals stirred and took on a deeper and deeper red, as if the flower were waking from a deathlike sleep. The thin stem and leaves became green, and there was the rose of half a century, looking as fresh as when Sylvia Ward had first given it to her lover. It was hardly fully open; some of its delicate red leaves curled modestly around its moist center, on which two or three drops of dew were sparkling.
“That is certainly a very pretty trick,” said the doctor’s friends, carelessly, because they had seen greater miracles at a magician’s show. “Pray, how was it done?”
“Did you never hear of the Fountain of Youth,” asked Dr. Heidegger, “which the Spanish explorer Ponce de León went in search of, two or three centuries ago?”
“But did Ponce de León ever find it?” said the Widow Wycherly.

“No,” answered Dr. Heidegger, “for he never looked in the right place. The famous Fountain of Youth, if I am correctly informed, is in the southern part of the Florida peninsula, not far from Lake Macaco. A friend of mine, knowing my curiosity in such matters, has sent me what you see in the vase.”
“Ahem!” said Colonel Killigrew, who believed not a word of the doctor’s story. “And what may be the effect of this fluid on the human body?”

“You shall judge for yourself, my dear Colonel,” replied Dr. Heidegger. “All of you, my respected friends, are welcome to as much of this wonderful fluid as may restore to you the bloom of youth. For my own part, having had so much trouble in growing old, I am in no hurry to grow young again. With your permission, therefore, I will merely watch the progress of the experiment.”

While he spoke, Dr. Heidegger had been filling the four champagne glasses with the water of the Fountain of Youth. Small bubbles were continually rising from the bottom of the glasses and bursting in silvery spray at the surface. A pleasant smell filled the room.

“Before you drink, my respectable old friends,” said the doctor, “it would be well that, with the experience of a lifetime to direct you, you should draw up a few general rules for your guidance, in passing a second time through the dangers of youth. Think what a sin and shame it would be if, with your special advantages, you did not become patterns of virtue and wisdom to all the young people of the age!”

The doctor’s four venerable friends made him no answer except a weak and trembling laugh. The idea was so very ridiculous, since they knew how closely regret follows on the steps of error, that they should ever go wrong again.
“Drink, then,” said the doctor, bowing. “I rejoice that I have so well selected the subjects of my experiment.”
With shaking hands, they raised the glasses to their lips. They drank off the water and put the glasses back on the table.

Immediately there was an improvement in the appearance of the party. A cheerful glow, like a burst of sunshine, brightened their faces. They looked at one another, and imagined that some magic power had really begun to smooth away the deep lines that Father Time had been carving on their faces for so long. The Widow Wycherly adjusted her cap, for she felt almost like a woman again.
“Give us more of this wonderful water!” they cried eagerly. “We are younger, but we are still too old! Quick! Give us more!”

“Patience, patience!” said Dr. Heidegger, who sat watching the experiment with scientific coolness. “You have been a long time growing old. Surely you might be content to grow young in half an hour! But the water is at your service.”

Again he filled their glasses. They drank it all at a single gulp. Was it an illusion? Even while the drink was passing down their throats, it seemed to have brought a change to their whole bodies. Their eyes grew clear and bright; a dark shade deepened among their silver hair. They sat around the table, three gentlemen of middle age, and a woman, hardly beyond her prime.
“My dear widow, you are charming!” cried Colonel Killigrew, whose eyes had been fixed on her face, while the shadows of age were flying from it like darkness from the red sunrise.

The fair widow knew, from long experience, that Colonel Killigrew’s compliments were not always measured by sober truth. So she rose and ran to the mirror, still afraid that the ugly face of an old woman would meet her eyes.

Meanwhile, the three gentlemen behaved in such a way as to prove that the water of the Fountain of Youth had some intoxicating qualities. Mr. Gascoigne’s mind seemed to run on political topics, though it was hard to say whether they belonged to the past, the present or the future, since the same ideas have been in fashion for fifty years. He talked loudly about patriotism and the people’s rights. Colonel Killigrew had been singing a happy drinking song and ringing his glass in time with the chorus, while his eyes moved toward the figure of the Widow Wycherly. On the other side of the table, Mr. Medbourne was busy with a calculation involving dollars and cents, and a plan to supply the East Indies with ice by harnessing a team of whales to the polar icebergs.

As for the Widow Wycherly, she stood before the mirror, smiling at her own image and greeting it as the friend whom she loved better than all the world. She put her face close to the glass to see whether some long-remembered wrinkle had really vanished. She examined whether the snow had so entirely melted from her hair that the old cap could be safely thrown aside. At last, turning quickly away, she came with a sort of dancing step to the table.
“My dear old doctor,” she cried, “please give me another glass!”
“Certainly, my dear madam, certainly!” replied the obliging doctor. “See! I have already filled the glasses.”

It was now near sunset, and the room had grown darker than ever. But a soft and moonlike glow came from within the vase, and rested equally on the four guests and on the doctor’s venerable figure. He sat in a high-backed, carved oak armchair, with a gray dignity of appearance that might have well suited Father Time himself, whose power had never been questioned except by this fortunate company. Even while drinking the third glass of the Fountain of Youth, they were almost frightened by the expression of his mysterious face.

But, the next moment, the exciting rush of young life shot through their veins. They were now in the happy prime of youth. Age, with its miserable train of cares and sorrows and diseases, was remembered only as the trouble of a dream, from which they had joyously woken. The fresh glow of the soul, so early lost, and without which the world’s successive scenes had been only a gallery of faded pictures, again threw its magic over all their prospects. They felt like new-created beings in a new-created universe.
“We are young! We are young!” they cried happily.

They were a group of merry young people, almost mad with the joyous energy of their age. They laughed loudly at their old-fashioned clothes, the wide-skirted coats and the gown of the young-old woman. One limped across the floor like a gouty grandfather. One set a pair of glasses on his nose and pretended to read the old black book. A third sat in an armchair and tried to imitate the venerable dignity of Dr. Heidegger. Then all shouted happily and leaped about the room.
The Widow Wycherly — if so fresh a young lady could be called a widow — tripped up to the doctor’s chair, with a mischievous merriment in her rosy face.
“Doctor, you dear old soul,” she cried, “get up and dance with me!” And then the four young people laughed louder than ever, to think what a strange figure the poor old doctor would make.
“Please excuse me,” answered the doctor quietly. “I am old and rheumatic, and my dancing days were over long ago. But any of these happy young gentlemen will be glad of so pretty a partner.”
“Dance with me, Clara!” cried Colonel Killigrew.
“No, no, I will be her partner!” shouted Mr. Gascoigne.
“She promised me her hand fifty years ago!” exclaimed Mr. Medbourne.

They all gathered around her. One caught both her hands in his passionate grasp; another threw his arm about her waist; the third buried his hand among the shiny curls under the widow’s cap. Blushing, struggling, scolding, laughing, her warm breath fanning each of their faces by turns, she tried to free herself, yet still remained in their triple embrace. Never was there a livelier picture of youthful rivalship, with bewitching beauty for the prize.

Yet, by a strange deception, owing to the darkness of the room and the antique clothes they still wore, the tall mirror is said to have reflected the figures of three old, gray, withered grandfathers, fighting foolishly for the shriveled ugliness of a gray old woman.

But they were young; their burning passions proved them so. Inflamed to madness by the flirting of the girl-widow, who neither gave nor quite withheld her favors, the three rivals began to exchange threatening glances. Still keeping hold of the fair prize, they grappled fiercely at one another’s throats. As they struggled back and forth, the table was overturned, and the vase dashed into a thousand fragments. The precious Water of Youth flowed in a bright stream across the floor, moistening the wings of a butterfly, which, grown old in the decline of summer, had alighted there to die. The insect fluttered lightly through the room and settled on the snowy head of Dr. Heidegger.
“Come, come, gentlemen! Come, Madame Wycherly,” exclaimed the doctor, “I really must protest against this riot.”

They stood still and shivered, for it seemed as if gray Time were calling them back from their sunny youth, far down into the chill and darksome vale of years. They looked at old Dr. Heidegger, who sat in his carved armchair, holding the rose of half a century, which he had rescued from among the fragments of the broken vase. At the motion of his hand, the four rioters resumed their seats, the more readily because their violent exertions had wearied them, youthful though they were.
“My poor Sylvia’s rose!” exclaimed Dr. Heidegger, holding it in the light of the sunset clouds. “It appears to be fading again.”

And so it was. Even while the party were looking at it, the flower continued to shrivel up, till it became as dry and fragile as when the doctor had first thrown it into the vase. He shook off the few drops of moisture which clung to its petals.

“I love it as well like this as in its dewy freshness,” he said, pressing the withered rose to his withered lips. While he spoke, the butterfly fluttered down from the doctor’s snowy head and fell upon the floor.

His guests shivered again. A strange coldness, whether of the body or the spirit they could not tell, was creeping gradually over them all. They looked at one another and imagined that each fleeting moment snatched away a charm and left a deepening line where none had been before. Was it an illusion? Had the changes of a lifetime been crowded into so brief a space, and were they now four aged people, sitting with their old friend, Dr. Heidegger?
“Are we grown old again, so soon?” they cried sadly.

In truth they had. The Water of Youth possessed merely a power more temporary than that of wine. The delirium which it created had passed away. Yes! They were old again. With a shuddering movement, the widow clasped her bony hands over her face, and wished that the coffin lid were over it, since it could no longer be beautiful.

“Yes, friends, you are old again,” said Dr. Heidegger, “and lo! the Water of Youth is all lavished on the ground. Well, I do not regret it. If the fountain gushed at my very doorstep, I would not stoop to bathe my lips in it — no, though its delirium were for years instead of moments. Such is the lesson you have taught me!”
But the doctor’s four friends had taught no such lesson to themselves. They resolved at once to make a pilgrimage to Florida, and drink at morning, noon and night from the Fountain of Youth.
